title: 12 Best RELAYTO Alternatives for 2026, by Use Case
summary: Compare the best RELAYTO alternatives for 2026 by job: interactive demos, flipbooks, and digital sales rooms, with real pricing and honest pros and cons.
body_markdown:
*Last updated: 2026.*


I run marketing at Storylane, so I evaluate RELAYTO alternatives most weeks. Here is the opinion this guide argues: "RELAYTO alternatives" is a trap phrase. RELAYTO does four genuinely different jobs, and almost every list ranking for this keyword shoves flipbook makers, digital sales rooms, and demo tools into one flat directory.


That helps nobody. The right RELAYTO alternative depends entirely on the job you are hiring the tool to do. This guide sorts 12 tools by job, publishes real starting prices, tells you when to just stay on RELAYTO, and shows exactly where Storylane fits and where it does not.


> **Definition:** A RELAYTO alternative is any tool you use instead of RELAYTO to turn static content into an interactive experience. Because RELAYTO spans four jobs, the "best" alternative is different for a demo team, a flipbook publisher, and a sales-enablement leader.


## Quick-pick summary: the best RELAYTO alternative for each need


Most buyers land here impatient. So before the deep dives, here is the short version. Match your primary job to the tool in the table, then read that tool's section for the honest pros and cons.


If you build interactive product demos, start with Storylane. If you publish flipbooks from PDFs, Publuu and FlippingBook lead on ratings. For a shared deal portal GetAccept owns the sales-room job, and if budget is the blocker Journey.io has a real free tier.


One caveat before you trust any at-a-glance table, including this one: a tool that tops the flipbook job will fail at the demo job, and the reverse is just as true. So read each "best pick" as the winner inside a job, not an overall crown. The sections below explain why each tool earns its spot, and where it quietly falls short.

## Why teams look for a RELAYTO alternative


RELAYTO is a capable interactive-content platform, and its 4.7 out of 5 rating across 470-plus reviews (G2, 2026) is earned. Teams still leave, and the reasons are consistent across the reviews and the sales conversations I see.


Three complaints recur across reviews and calls:


- The learning curve is steep and the interface confusing for occasional builders.
- Documentation and support feel thin once you get past the basics.
- Pricing is premium, with no transparent public list prices for the core tiers, which stalls procurement.


Reviewers also flag two practical issues: no dedicated mobile app, and slower performance on large, media-heavy files. If your team publishes big, image-dense experiences, test that before committing.


Underneath the feature complaints sits a deeper mismatch. Many buyers are trying to escape a video-first or manual workflow that only imitates interactivity. One put it bluntly:


> "I'm having to record video clips to sort of give the illusion of interactivity."
>
>
> \[product support lead, cybersecurity\]


That is the real trigger: people do not want more clips to maintain, they want a genuinely interactive experience that updates in minutes, not days. If you are still stitching screen recordings together, our take on[SaaS product demo videos](https://www.storylane.io/blog/saas-product-demo-and-explainer-videos) explains why the format caps out.


Cost sharpens the urgency, especially after a bad bet. As one buyer told us, a wasted subscription made the next decision about price, not features.


> "The lower cost is going to create less of a barrier for entry to this, because I think we've just wasted like nine months of money in Synthesia."
>
>
> \[product support lead, cybersecurity\]


> **Who should stay on RELAYTO:** if your core job is publishing rich, multimedia microsites and interactive magazines, and your team already knows the tool, switching buys you little. The tools below win when your job is demos, sales rooms, or cheap, fast flipbooks, not when RELAYTO already fits.


## What RELAYTO actually does, and the 4 jobs people hire it for


Here is the disambiguation that no ranked page bothers with. "RELAYTO alternatives" returns wildly different tools because RELAYTO itself is used for four separate jobs. Buy for the wrong job and every comparison misleads you.


The four jobs are:


1. **Flipbooks and microsites:** turning PDFs, decks, and reports into page-flip experiences or lightweight web pages.
2. **Interactive content experiences:** building clickable, media-rich content that tracks engagement, RELAYTO's home turf.
3. **Digital sales rooms:** sharing a curated, single-link portal of assets with a buying committee.
4. **Interactive product demos:** letting prospects click through your actual product, self-guided.


Those jobs need different engines: a flipbook tool cannot capture your product UI, and a demo platform is overkill for a page-flip catalog. This is why the[interactive demo software](https://www.storylane.io/blog/interactive-demo-software) category and the flipbook category rarely belong in the same list.


The sales-room job is the one buyers describe most vividly. One marketing manager wanted a single curated link rather than a folder of attachments:


> "How is it that you can share a portal with them which has a list of all this information and in a very curated way so that it becomes very user friendly for them to see which information they want."
>
>
> \[marketing manager, IT services\]


Decide your primary job first. Then, and only then, read the section built for it.


## How we evaluated these RELAYTO alternatives


I did not rank a flat "best." I scored each tool inside its job, using criteria that actually predict whether a team keeps a tool past month three.


- **Primary job:** which of the four jobs the tool is genuinely built for, not merely tolerates.
- **Pricing transparency:** whether a starting price and free-plan status are public, so procurement can move without a sales call.
- **Ease of use and time to first output:** how fast a non-technical builder ships something real, since a steep curve is the top reason teams churn.
- **Analytics depth:** whether you can see who engaged with what, which is the point of interactive content.
- **Integrations:** CRM, CMS, and enablement connections that fit an existing stack.
- **Ideal team size:** solo publisher, growing team, or enterprise with governance and security-review needs.


Two criteria deserve emphasis because they surface in nearly every deal. First, evaluate migration and onboarding directly: ask any vendor how a current RELAYTO library gets rebuilt and how long the first week takes. Second, evaluate governance early, because multi-stakeholder buy-in and a security review will gate the purchase whether or not the demo dazzled.


## Best RELAYTO alternatives for interactive product demos


If your job is letting prospects click through your real product, this is your section. These tools capture your live UI and turn it into a guided, self-serve experience. For a broader field, see our roundup of the[best sales demo tools](https://www.storylane.io/blog/best-sales-demo-tools) .


### Storylane


Full disclosure: this is us. Storylane is a purpose-built interactive demo platform, and it is the strongest all-rounder in this section for guided product tours and self-serve demos. You capture your product by screen recording or by HTML capture, then edit it in a real demo editor, add guided tooltips, and publish to Demo Hubs, our category take on[product tour software](https://www.storylane.io/blog/product-tour-software) .


The mechanism matters more than the marketing. Because Storylane captures the actual UI and lets you edit the HTML, you build one comprehensive demo and re-cut tailored versions per client instead of re-recording. Sandbox Demos let prospects explore freely, and analytics show which screens a buyer leaned into before the call. That controlled exposure is exactly what one buyer wanted:


> "The more you have to open the kimono and expose everything, the more we're going to pick it apart and the longer we're going to have time."
>
>
> \[solutions & architecture director, networking\]


The payoff shows up on the page. One customer described an interactive experience lifting results sharply:


> "This specific one increased the conversion on the page with almost three times."
>
>
> \[product marketing director, martech\]


It also fixes the clunky live handoff between an explainer and the real product that trade-show teams complain about. Where Storylane does not fit: if your only job is publishing a page-flip PDF catalog or a media-heavy magazine, this is the wrong tool, and you should buy a flipbook maker instead. Storylane offers a free plan to start, so you can test the demo job before you commit.


### Supademo


Supademo is a clean, lightweight interactive-demo tool and the closest editorial competitor for this keyword. It is genuinely easy to start, and it prices low: around $27 per month (as of 2026), which buyers notice. One told us Supademo ran roughly $12 a month cheaper than the comparable alternative, so on pure entry cost it competes hard.


The trade-off is depth. Supademo shines for quick, single-flow demos and help-center walkthroughs, while larger teams that need heavy governance, many re-cut variants, and deeper analytics tend to outgrow it. Best for solo builders and small teams who want fast, affordable demos over an enterprise demo program.


### Consensus


Consensus is built for buyer-led, on-demand demos in the pre-sales process, and it has been in market longer than most. Its strength is scaling a "watch the demo yourself" motion across a buying committee, so if your pain is that too many demos require a live human, it attacks that directly. Compare it against the field in our[Consensus alternatives](https://www.storylane.io/blog/consensus-alternatives) guide.


The honest limit is format. Consensus grew up video-first, and that still shapes the work, as one buyer noted:


> "Consensus has been around the longest, but they've been focused on video for that whole time, it still means you have to make the videos like that."
>
>
> \[role not captured, segment not captured\]


Best for teams that want intelligent demo automation and are comfortable producing video, less so for teams that want a fully clickable, editable product replica.


### Navattic and Walnut


Navattic and Walnut are the two demo tools buyers most often compare against the others here. Navattic is a solid no-code interactive demo builder; a buyer told us its subscriptions start at $125 per month, with a growth tier around $1,000 per month before discounting. Its gap, in one buyer's words, is editing depth:


> "There's no demo editor, so being able to edit the HTML is a key growth thing."
>
>
> \[security specialist, cybersecurity\]


Walnut sits at the enterprise end, and it prices there: one buyer reported paying roughly $25,000. Best for large teams with the budget and the demand for a heavily managed demo program. If you want editable HTML capture and a lower entry point, weigh that against both.


## Best RELAYTO alternatives for flipbooks and PDF conversion


If you treat RELAYTO as a way to turn PDFs and decks into page-flip experiences, you want a dedicated flipbook maker, not a demo platform. These four dominate the directory results and do the job cheaply.


Tool Starting price Free plan G2 rating Best for


FlippingBook from ~$19/mo Trial only 4.7 (G2, 298 reviews) Polished, trackable flipbooks


Issuu Free, then paid Yes n/a Publishing and distribution reach


Publuu from ~$15/mo Trial only 4.8 (G2, 558 reviews) Fast, good-looking flipbooks


Flipsnack from ~$14/mo Yes 4.7 (G2, 411 reviews) Design control and catalogs


**Publuu** earns the highest rating in this group at 4.8 out of 5 across 558 reviews (G2, 2026). It converts a PDF into a flipbook in minutes and adds lightweight tracking, which is why it leads the quick-pick for this job.


**FlippingBook** is the professional's choice, rated 4.7 across 298 reviews (G2, 2026). It focuses on branded, secure, trackable documents and integrates with common marketing tools. **Flipsnack** rates 4.7 across 411 reviews (G2, 2026) and adds strong design control plus a free tier, which suits catalogs. **Issuu** is the reach play: a large publishing network and a genuine free plan, best when distribution matters more than deep analytics. None of these captures a product UI, so do not buy them for demos.


## Best RELAYTO alternatives for digital sales rooms and sales enablement


If your job is sharing one curated portal of content with a buying committee, you are in the digital sales room category. This is the "curated portal" a buyer described earlier, and it is a different tool class again. Our[digital sales room software](https://www.storylane.io/blog/digital-sales-room-software) breakdown goes deeper.


**GetAccept** is the strongest all-round pick here, rated 4.6 across 1,267 reviews (G2, 2026). It combines digital sales rooms with e-signature and deal tracking, so a rep runs the whole late-stage deal from one link. Pricing is quote-based, which is the norm at this tier.


**Showpad** is the enterprise sales-enablement suite, rated 4.6 across 1,900-plus reviews (G2, 2026). It fits large teams that need content governance, training, and analytics together, and it prices and implements accordingly. **Paperflite** , rated 4.7 across 340 reviews (G2, 2026), is the nimbler content-management and sales-room option for growing teams that want engagement tracking without the enterprise weight.


**Tourial and Journey.io** blur the line between demo and sales room. Journey.io is a flexible, affordable way to assemble content and demos into a shareable buyer page. Tourial targets marketing-led interactive experiences at roughly $600 to $1,000 per month. One buyer was candid about the switching cost of the wrong pick here:


> "I've been a real bitter Betty about having to migrate everything \[Tourial\] that I don't even like."
>
>
> \[product marketing director, HR software\]


That line is the whole case for evaluating migration before you sign, not after.


## Best free and low-cost RELAYTO alternatives


Price is the single most common reason teams leave RELAYTO, and none of the top-ranking pages breaks out the cheap options as their own section. Here are the tools with a real free plan or a sub-$30 entry point.


- **Journey.io:** a genuine free tier, then paid plans at $29, $49, and $79 per user (as of 2026). The best free starting point for assembling buyer-facing pages.
- **Storylane:** offers a free plan to start building interactive demos, so you can prove the job before you budget for it.
- **Supademo:** around $27 per month (as of 2026), the low-cost pick for straightforward demos.
- **Flipsnack and Issuu:** both offer free flipbook tiers if you only need occasional PDF conversion.
- **Publuu:** low monthly entry from about $15 for polished flipbooks.


A worked example on why cheap-to-start matters. A cybersecurity team told us they had effectively lost nine months of spend on a mismatched tool before switching, so their next decision led with price and low barrier to entry. Starting on a free or sub-$30 plan lets you validate the job with real prospects before you spend, which is exactly the de-risking that story argues for.

## How to choose the right RELAYTO alternative


Skip the feature spreadsheet at first. Start with the job, because the job eliminates most of the field instantly. Use this decision path.


- **If you need interactive product demos,** choose Storylane for editable capture and re-cut variants, Supademo if budget leads and flows are simple, or Consensus if you want buyer-led, on-demand demos.
- **If you need flipbooks or PDF conversion,** choose Publuu or FlippingBook for polish and tracking, Flipsnack for design control, or Issuu for distribution reach.
- **If you need a digital sales room,** choose GetAccept for deal-stage selling, Showpad if you need enterprise enablement and training, or Journey.io if you want a free, flexible start.
- **If price is the hard constraint,** start free on Journey.io or Storylane, or pay under $30 for Supademo or a flipbook maker.


Then pressure-test three things every buying committee eventually raises. Ask how migration and onboarding actually work so week one produces something real, and ask what security and compliance review the vendor supports, because that gate is coming. Finally, ask for transparent pricing you can take to procurement without a second call.


A quick worked example: a retail POS marketer told us they were rebuilding their website "focusing on conversion opportunities," and separately wanted a short product tour a CSM could share to expand accounts into a new module. That is two demo jobs, so a demo platform wins, not a flipbook tool. Match the tool to the job and the shortlist writes itself.


## Frequently asked questions


**What is the best RELAYTO alternative?**


There is no single best, because RELAYTO does four jobs. For interactive product demos Storylane is the strongest all-rounder, for flipbooks Publuu and FlippingBook lead on ratings, and for digital sales rooms GetAccept is the top pick. Match the tool to your primary job first.


**Is there a free RELAYTO alternative?**


Yes. Journey.io has a genuine free tier, Storylane offers a free plan for building interactive demos, and on the flipbook side Issuu and Flipsnack both offer free plans. These let you validate the job with real prospects before you spend.


**Why is RELAYTO so expensive?**


RELAYTO does not publish public list prices for its core tiers, and reviewers describe the pricing as premium. That opacity is a common reason procurement stalls and teams shop alternatives. If transparent pricing matters, prioritize tools that publish a starting price, such as Supademo, Journey.io, or the flipbook makers.


**What is the difference between RELAYTO and an interactive demo tool?**


RELAYTO builds interactive content experiences and microsites from documents and media. An interactive demo tool like Storylane captures your actual product UI and turns it into a clickable, self-guided demo. If you need prospects to experience the product, not read about it, a demo tool is the right category.


**Does RELAYTO have a mobile app?**


Reviewers consistently note that RELAYTO does not offer a dedicated mobile app, and some report slower performance on large, media-heavy files. If mobile creation or editing is important to your team, confirm current capabilities with the vendor and test with your real files before committing.


## Conclusion and recommendation


The honest recommendation is the one no ranked page will give you: the best RELAYTO alternative is the one built for your specific job, and sometimes that answer is to stay on RELAYTO. Decide the job first, then price and features become easy.


If your job is interactive product demos, I am biased but confident that Storylane is where to start, and the free plan means you risk nothing to find out. If your job is flipbooks or sales rooms, pick from those sections instead. Buy for the job, not for the list.


Whatever you shortlist, run the same three checks before you sign: how migration off RELAYTO actually works, what security and compliance review the vendor supports, and whether pricing is transparent enough to clear procurement. A tool that wins the demo and loses those three will stall in the buying committee. Get the job and the checks right, and the decision stops feeling like a gamble.
